analysis.one_liner: Restricts Medicare Advantage plans' use of prior authorization and claims denials.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced September 15, 2026, has one cosponsor and sits without action in two House committees while Congress finishes its session in January 2027.
analysis.plain_summary: Medicare Advantage plans, run by private insurers, must often approve care in advance ('prior authorization') and can deny claims after the fact. This bill would set new requirements on how those plans use prior authorization and how they deny claims under Medicare. It was referred to two House committees with jurisdiction over Medicare and has had no further action.
analysis.who_benefits: Seniors enrolled in Medicare Advantage plans, who face delays or denials when plans require advance approval for care or reject claims for treatment already received. Doctors and hospitals also benefit when fewer services are delayed or denied.

how_it_helps.text: The bill would establish requirements for how Medicare Advantage plans use prior authorization and handle claims denials under Medicare [S1].
Prior authorization requirements are a well-known source of delayed or denied care for Medicare Advantage enrollees; tightening the rules would reduce those barriers for people in these plans.

The bill covers both halves of Medicare's private-insurer program's jurisdiction, having been referred to both Ways and Means and Energy and Commerce, the two committees that share oversight of Medicare [S1].

analysis.who_pays: Medicare Advantage insurers, which would face new federal restrictions on their use of prior authorization and claims denials, potentially increasing their costs and limiting one tool they use to control spending. If insurers cannot control costs this way, some of that cost could show up in premiums or plan offerings.

drawbacks.text: Insurers and some health policy analysts argue prior authorization, used properly, deters unnecessary procedures and holds down costs; tightening it could push costs back onto the Medicare program or into premiums, and could lead some insurers to scale back their Medicare Advantage offerings.
The bill has minimal stated detail in the public summary about what the new requirements would be, so it is hard to judge the strength or enforceability of the protections it would create [S1].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For seniors, the benefit of fewer delayed or denied claims is concrete and directly felt. The main counterweight is that insurers argue prior authorization controls costs, and stricter rules could raise plan costs or reduce plan choices. On balance, the bill targets a process widely criticized for delaying needed care, but its low-cosponsor support and lack of committee action leave its actual design and prospects unresolved.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in mid-September 2026 and sent to two House committees with jurisdiction over Medicare, and neither committee has taken any action on it since.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced in the House on September 15, 2026 [S1].
On the day of introduction it was referred to the Committee on Ways and Means and to the Committee on Energy and Commerce, which share jurisdiction over Medicare provisions [S3].
It has one cosponsor, a Republican, alongside its Democratic sponsor [S2].
No further action — no hearings, markups, or votes — appears in the bill's action history [S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Medicare Advantage insurers, which continue to operate without new restrictions on prior authorization or claims denials while the bill sits without action in committee.

for.name: Rep. Greg Landsman
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to set requirements on Medicare Advantage plans' use of prior authorization and claims denials [S1].

against.name: House Ways and Means and Energy and Commerce Committees
against.role: Committees with jurisdiction over Medicare provisions
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on the day of introduction and have taken no action — no hearing, markup, or vote — since [S3].

sides.party_line_note: The bill has two members total: one Democratic sponsor and one Republican cosponsor [S2].

industries.note: The bill would restrict the tools — prior authorization and claims denials — that these insurers use to manage and limit spending on care for enrolled seniors. Their interest in blocking or weakening the bill runs against seniors' interest in faster, fewer denials of care.
Fewer prior authorization delays and claim denials mean faster payment and less administrative burden fighting denials, alongside better care flow for patients.

analysis.trajectory: Introduced mid-September with one cosponsor and no committee action in either committee of referral, the bill is unlikely to see a hearing or vote before this Congress ends January 3, 2027; it would need to be reintroduced to continue.
